issues.legal_issue: A collateral claiming succession to a father's self-acquired property must establish a binding special local custom that excludes the daughter from the general rule preferring her.
material_facts: The dispute concerned non-ancestral property left by a deceased father, claimed by his daughter and by a collateral within the fourth degree.
The collateral relied on a local custom said to exclude the daughter from succession to the father's self-acquired property.
The Court found that the collateral had not established the alleged special local custom.
issues.conclusion: The general custom preferring a daughter to collaterals in succession to her father's self-acquired property applied, and the daughter succeeded to the non-ancestral property.
issues.legal_principle: Paragraph 23(2) of Rattigan's Digest states the general Punjab custom that a daughter succeeds to her father's self-acquired property in preference to collaterals, even those within the fourth degree. The Court approved that rule, relying on Gopal Singh v. Ujagar Singh, and held, consistently with Mst. Subhani v. Nawab, that the initial onus is on collaterals to prove a binding special local custom varying the general rule.

rule.if: succession_dispute and property_is_self_acquired and competing_claimant_is_daughter and claimant_is_collateral_within_fourth_degree and not reliable_proof_of_excluding_local_custom

predicates.succession_dispute: A proceeding concerns competing claims to succession to a deceased person's property.
predicates.property_is_self_acquired: The property at issue was acquired by the deceased rather than inherited as ancestral property.
predicates.competing_claimant_is_daughter: A daughter of the deceased claims succession to the property.
predicates.claimant_is_collateral_within_fourth_deg: A collateral related to the deceased within the fourth degree claims the property.
predicates.reliable_proof_of_excluding_local_custom: Reliable evidence establishes a binding local custom that excludes the daughter from succession to the self-acquired property.

issues.definition: When a succession dispute concerns a daughter's claim to self-acquired property against a collateral within the fourth degree, and no reliable proof establishes an excluding local custom, the daughter is preferred.

issues.legal_issue: A record of local custom does not displace the general rule preferring a daughter if it is unreliable and untrustworthy as evidence of the custom it purports to record.
material_facts: The collateral relied on a district record of custom whose answers stated that daughters were excluded by male kindred and that no distinction was made between ancestral and self-acquired property.
The record's compiler acknowledged that people had sometimes stated what the custom should be rather than what it actually was.
The record contained collected instances of daughters inheriting, and its answers on daughters' succession had been contradicted and discredited in judicial proceedings.
The disputed entries adversely affected women's rights, although women had no opportunity to appear before the revenue authorities.
issues.conclusion: The district records were not reliable or trustworthy on daughters' succession to self-acquired property, had no presumptive value on that question, and did not shift the initial burden from the collateral to the daughter.
issues.legal_principle: Riwaj-i-am entries receive an initial presumption of correctness, but the evidence needed to rebut that presumption depends on the circumstances. The presumption is weaker when the recorded custom conflicts with the general custom or adversely affects women who had no opportunity to participate. Under Qamar-ud-Din v. Mt. Fateh Bano, a record can support a special custom if it is reliable and trustworthy, carefully prepared, free of internal contradictions, and not merely a record of what respondents wished the custom to be; an unreliable record has no presumptive value. The Court also relied on the principles in Beg v. Allah Ditta, Mt. Vaishno Ditti v. Mt. Rameshri, Khan Beg v. Mt. Fateh Khatun, Jagat Singh v. Mst. Jiwan, Mst. Subhani v. Nawab, and Mohammad Khalil v. Mohammad Bakhsh.

rule.if: succession_dispute and record_claims_custom_excluding_daughter and (record_conflicts_with_general_custom or record_adversely_affects_unrepresented_women) and compiler_doubted_actual_custom and record_contains_contrary_instances and record_was_discredited_in_judicial_proceedings

predicates.succession_dispute: A proceeding concerns competing claims to succession to a deceased person's property.
predicates.record_claims_custom_excluding_daughter: A record of custom states that male kindred exclude a daughter from succession.
predicates.record_conflicts_with_general_custom: The custom stated in the record conflicts with the generally prevailing custom on the succession in dispute.
predicates.record_adversely_affects_unrepresented_w: The recorded custom adversely affects women who had no opportunity to participate in its recording.
predicates.compiler_doubted_actual_custom: The compiler stated that respondents sometimes described what the custom should be rather than what it actually was.
predicates.record_contains_contrary_instances: The record includes instances inconsistent with the custom stated in its answers.
predicates.record_was_discredited_in_judicial_proce: Courts had previously rejected the record's statements on the relevant custom as incorrect.

issues.definition: When a succession record claims an excluding custom but conflicts with the general custom or adversely affects unrepresented women, and its compiler doubted its accuracy, it contains contrary instances, and courts had discredited it, the record has no presumptive value.
